items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a visitor who travels to a country other than their own and stays at least one night”.
items.answer: International tourist arrival
items.markingKey: International tourist arrival: a visitor who travels to a country other than their own and stays at least one night. [1]

items.stem: Explain the reasons for the growth of international tourism.
items.answer: Rising incomes and paid holidays; cheaper and faster air travel (jumbo jets, low-cost carriers); package holidays; internet booking; growth of the middle class in China and India; marketing; visa relaxation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per reason [4]

items.stem: Describe the global pattern of international tourism.
items.answer: Europe receives about half of arrivals; Asia-Pacific has grown fastest; the Americas next; Africa and the Middle East have small shares; most tourism is between HICs and within regions.

items.stem: Fig. 25.1 shows international tourist arrivals (millions): 1950: 25, 1980: 278, 1990: 435, 2000: 674, 2010: 952, 2019: 1465, 2020: 407, 2023: 1300. Explain why arrivals fell in 2020 and recovered slowly.
items.answer: COVID-19 border closures, quarantine rules and flight cancellations; afterwards lost incomes, health fears, slow reopening in Asia and staff shortages.

items.stem: Fig. 25.1 shows international tourist arrivals (millions): 1950: 25, 1980: 278, 1990: 435, 2000: 674, 2010: 952, 2019: 1465, 2020: 407, 2023: 1300. (a) Calculate the percentage change in arrivals between 2019 and 2020. (b) Explain why arrivals fell in 2020 and recovered slowly.
items.answer: (a) −72.2% (b) COVID-19 border closures, quarantine rules and flight cancellations; afterwards lost incomes, health fears, slow reopening in Asia and staff shortages.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that the growth of international tourism is mainly the result of improvements in transport?
items.answer: For: Jet aircraft, wide-bodied jets and low-cost airlines cut journey times and costs, extending the pleasure periphery. Against: Rising incomes, paid holidays, the internet, marketing, the growth of the middle class in Asia, political changes and visa policies also drove growth. Conclusion: Transport made long-distance tourism possible, but rising incomes and leisure time created the demand.

items.stem: Explain why tourism is vulnerable to external shocks.
items.answer: It depends on travel, confidence and disposable income: pandemics, terrorism, natural disasters, recessions, conflict and oil prices quickly reduce arrivals.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the process by which tourist spending creates further rounds of income and jobs as money circulates in the local economy”.
items.answer: Tourism multiplier
items.markingKey: Tourism multiplier: the process by which tourist spending creates further rounds of income and jobs as money circulates in the local economy. [1]

items.stem: Explain the tourism multiplier effect.
items.answer: Tourist spending creates direct jobs and income in hotels and attractions; suppliers gain indirect income; employees spend their wages locally (induced effect); tax revenue funds infrastructure, attracting more visitors.

items.stem: Explain the stages of the Butler model.
items.answer: Exploration (few adventurous visitors); involvement (local facilities); development (rapid growth, external investment); consolidation (growth slows); stagnation (capacity reached, reputation falls); then decline or rejuvenation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per stage [4]

items.stem: International tourists spent US$300 million in Jamaica in one year. About 27% of this spending leaked out of the economy immediately. Of the income that remains, local people re-spend about 51% locally; each round of spending also leaks 27%. The multiplier k = 1 ÷ (1 − 0.51 × (1 − 0.27)). Explain why leakage is high in many small tourist destinations.
items.answer: Foreign-owned hotels and airlines send profits abroad; food, drink and building materials are imported; foreign managers; all-inclusive packages paid in the source country.

items.stem: International tourists spent US$300 million in Kenya’s coast in one year. About 46% of this spending leaked out of the economy immediately. Of the income that remains, local people re-spend about 53% locally; each round of spending also leaks 46%. The multiplier k = 1 ÷ (1 − 0.53 × (1 − 0.46)). (a) Calculate the spending retained after initial leakage. (b) Calculate the multiplier and the total income generated in the local economy.
items.answer: (a) US$162 million (b) k = 1.4; total US$227 million

items.stem: International tourists spent US$300 million in Bali, Indonesia in one year. About 47% of this spending leaked out of the economy immediately. Of the income that remains, local people re-spend about 41% locally; each round of spending also leaks 47%. The multiplier k = 1 ÷ (1 − 0.41 × (1 − 0.47)). (a) Calculate the spending retained after initial leakage. (b) Suggest how the destination could increase the multiplier effect.
items.answer: (a) US$159 million (b) Encourage local ownership and suppliers (local food), train local staff for management jobs, limit all-inclusives, promote local crafts and excursions, tax foreign operators.

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that the Butler model is useful for managing tourist destinations. In your answer you may refer to rejuvenation and shocks.
items.answer: For: It identifies warning signs of stagnation and the need for planning, diversification and carrying-capacity limits (e.g. Benidorm, Blackpool). Against: Many destinations do not follow its stages; it is hard to apply predictively; external shocks dominate; it is better as a description than a management tool. Conclusion: The model is a helpful framework for thinking about change, but managers need detailed local data to use it.

items.stem: Explain the negative impacts of mass tourism on destinations.
items.answer: Overcrowding and congestion; rising house prices and loss of residents (Venice); damage to ecosystems and heritage; water shortages; waste and pollution; seasonal, low-paid jobs; cultural erosion.

items.stem: Explain how tourist destinations can be managed sustainably.
items.answer: Visitor limits and pricing; zoning; local ownership and employment; environmental regulations; investment of revenue in conservation; diversifying the season; community involvement.

items.stem: Briefly describe how tourism in the destination is managed, for Venice, Italy or another example of the management of a tourist destination.
items.answer: Venice, Italy: Ban on large cruise ships in the lagoon centre (2021); day-tripper access fee (2024, €5, raised to €10 for late bookings in 2025); limits on group sizes; restrictions on new hotels and short-term lets; MOSE flood barriers protect the city and its tourism.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 4 marks for accurate, place-specific points (names, dates, figures), max 2 if general. Named policies, dates, fees and organisations. [5]

items.stem: Using a named example of the management of a tourist destination you have studied, assess how sustainable the management of tourism has been.
items.answer: Model answer (Bhutan): High value, low volume policy since 1974; Sustainable Development Fee (US$200 per night from 2022, reduced to US$100 in 2023); licensed guides; protected areas cover about half of the country; constitutional requirement for 60% forest cover. Culture and environment are well protected and fees fund health and education; but high costs limit arrivals and income, and tourism recovery after COVID-19 was slow.

items.stem: Assess the view that sustainable tourism is an unrealistic goal for most tourist destinations. In your answer you may refer to overtourism, visitor management and climate change.
items.answer: For: Mass tourism brings overtourism, leakage and environmental damage; long-haul flights cause emissions; destinations depend on growth (Venice, Maldives). Against: High-value, low-volume (Bhutan), community-based tourism, visitor management (Machu Picchu) and local ownership show sustainable approaches can work. Conclusion: Full sustainability is difficult, especially with air travel, but management can make tourism much more sustainable.

items.stem: Referring to Venice, Italy or another example of the management of a tourist destination, assess how sustainable the management of tourism has been.
items.answer: Model answer (Venice, Italy): Ban on large cruise ships in the lagoon centre (2021); day-tripper access fee (2024, €5, raised to €10 for late bookings in 2025); limits on group sizes; restrictions on new hotels and short-term lets; MOSE flood barriers protect the city and its tourism. Cruise traffic in the centre stopped and the fee raised revenue, but visitor numbers on fee days fell little, the resident population of the historic centre has fallen below 50 000, and UNESCO has warned about overtourism.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the spending of international visitors in a country”.
items.answer: Tourism receipts

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “China has become the largest source of international tourist spending.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) A student writes: “Most international tourists travel to LICs.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Chinese outbound spending grew rapidly before 2020. (b) Not correct. Most visit HICs, particularly in Europe.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Describe the global pattern of international tourism. (b) A revision website states: “International arrivals recovered fully to 2019 levels in 2021.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Europe receives about half of arrivals; Asia-Pacific has grown fastest; the Americas next; Africa and the Middle East have small shares; most tourism is between HICs and within regions. (b) Not correct. Recovery took until about 2024.
items.markingKey: (a) [3] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Fig. 25.1 shows international tourist arrivals (millions): 1950: 25, 1980: 278, 1990: 435, 2000: 674, 2010: 952, 2019: 1465, 2020: 407, 2023: 1300. International tourists spent US$300 million in the Gambia in one year. About 54% of this spending leaked out of the economy immediately. Of the income that remains, local people re-spend about 51% locally; each round of spending also leaks 54%. The multiplier k = 1 ÷ (1 − 0.51 × (1 − 0.54)). (a) Calculate the spending retained after initial leakage. (b) Calculate the multiplier and the total income generated in the local economy.
items.answer: (a) US$138 million (b) k = 1.31; total US$180.3 million

items.stem: Fig. 25.1 shows international tourist arrivals (millions): 1950: 25, 1980: 278, 1990: 435, 2000: 674, 2010: 952, 2019: 1465, 2020: 407, 2023: 1300. (a) Calculate arrivals in 2023 as a percentage of the 2019 level. (b) Explain the growth in arrivals between 1950 and 2019.
items.answer: (a) 88.7% (b) Rising incomes and paid holidays, cheaper air travel, package and low-cost holidays, internet booking, growth of Asian middle classes and new destinations.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a model (1980) showing how a resort passes through exploration, involvement, development, consolidation, stagnation and then decline or rejuvenation”.
items.answer: Butler model (tourist area life cycle)
items.markingKey: Butler model (tourist area life cycle): a model (1980) showing how a resort passes through exploration, involvement, development, consolidation, stagnation and then decline or rejuvenation. [1]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A student writes: “All tourist spending stays in the destination.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain the stages of the Butler model.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Much leaks out through imports and foreign ownership. (b) Exploration (few adventurous visitors); involvement (local facilities); development (rapid growth, external investment); consolidation (growth slows); stagnation (capacity reached, reputation falls); then decline or rejuvenation.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark per stage [4]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A revision website states: “The Butler model predicts exact dates for each stage.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain the tourism multiplier effect.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. It is descriptive; timings differ between resorts. (b) Tourist spending creates direct jobs and income in hotels and attractions; suppliers gain indirect income; employees spend their wages locally (induced effect); tax revenue funds infrastructure, attracting more visitors.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) [4]

items.stem: International tourists spent US$300 million in Kenya’s coast in one year. About 28% of this spending leaked out of the economy immediately. Of the income that remains, local people re-spend about 69% locally; each round of spending also leaks 28%. The multiplier k = 1 ÷ (1 − 0.69 × (1 − 0.28)). items.stem: What is meant by the term “overtourism”?
options: A daily charge on most international visitors to Bhutan to fund conservation and public services.
Tourism owned or managed by local communities so that benefits stay local.
A charge introduced in 2024 for day visitors entering Venice’s historic centre on peak days.
When visitor numbers exceed the capacity of a destination, harming residents’ quality of life and the environment.
items.answer: When visitor numbers exceed the capacity of a destination, harming residents’ quality of life and the environment.
items.markingKey: Overtourism: when visitor numbers exceed the capacity of a destination, harming residents’ quality of life and the environment. [1]

items.stem: A revision website states: “Ecotourism has no environmental impact.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Flights and visitor activities still cause impacts.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain the negative impacts of mass tourism on destinations. (b) A revision website states: “Ecotourism has no environmental impact.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Overcrowding and congestion; rising house prices and loss of residents (Venice); damage to ecosystems and heritage; water shortages; waste and pollution; seasonal, low-paid jobs; cultural erosion. (b) Not correct. Flights and visitor activities still cause impacts.

items.stem: Briefly describe how tourism in the destination is managed, for Bhutan or another example of the management of a tourist destination.
items.answer: Bhutan: High value, low volume policy since 1974; Sustainable Development Fee (US$200 per night from 2022, reduced to US$100 in 2023); licensed guides; protected areas cover about half of the country; constitutional requirement for 60% forest cover.

items.stem: Using one named example of the management of a tourist destination, describe how tourism in the destination is managed.
items.answer: the Maldives: One island, one resort model separating resorts from local communities; rules limiting building heights and coverage; marine protected areas; guesthouse tourism on local islands since 2009; green tax on tourists.

items.stem: “Sustainable tourism is an unrealistic goal for most tourist destinations.” Discuss.
items.answer: For: Mass tourism brings overtourism, leakage and environmental damage; long-haul flights cause emissions; destinations depend on growth (Venice, Maldives). Against: High-value, low-volume (Bhutan), community-based tourism, visitor management (Machu Picchu) and local ownership show sustainable approaches can work. Conclusion: Full sustainability is difficult, especially with air travel, but management can make tourism much more sustainable.
